output.text: Compiled 42 candidate manuscripts, including 16 with evidence for three or more content categories: 26 fully digitised, 4 partially digitised, and 12 catalogue-only. The corpus records dating and provenance uncertainties, category-specific evidence, access links, 101 near-misses, coverage gaps, and limits to exhaustiveness.

Broad 15th-century, mid-century and third-quarter datings are retained when they overlap 1400–1455; they do not prove copying before 1455. Coverage is strongest for Alsace/Haguenau, Swabia, Lake Constance and broadly Alemannic or southwestern German production. No additional explicitly localized qualifying pre-1455 Vorarlberg or Schaffhausen witness was established. These are discovery gaps, not assertions of historical absence.

Precisely localized and dated 1400–1420 and 1451–1455 witnesses remain sparse. Unit-level watermarks, palaeography and binding history need further examination, particularly in composites.

Some records explicitly identify indirect content evidence based on the documented structure of a complete textual version rather than a manuscript-level chapter inventory. These need image-level checking; a title alone is not treated as adequate evidence.

Catalogue-only means no manuscript-image resource was verified, not proof that none exists. Partially digitised includes isolated reproductions and resources whose completeness could not be verified. Catalogue-only discoveries are retained separately from available facsimiles.

structured.exhaustion_assessment: The discovery corpus contains 42 distinct shelfmarks, including explicitly flagged uncertain-date and uncertain-geography candidates; 16 have evidence for three or more requested content categories. Access is classified as 26 fully digitised, 4 partially digitised and 12 catalogue-only. Discovery combined e-codices, e-manuscripta, Swisscollections, Handschriftencensus, KdiH, Handschriftenportal-linked descriptions, institutional digital libraries, ARCA/IRHT, older printed catalogue references and scholarly text-transmission resources. Mirrors were reconciled by shelfmark, and distinct shelfmarks remain separate. Later additions were not used to manufacture an early mixed-content witness. Follow-up searches addressed geographic gaps, unillustrated/Latin material, botanical glossaries, displaced codices, broad-date overlaps and incunable-bound working books; these increasingly produced duplicates or unresolved/non-qualifying leads. This suggests substantial saturation of readily searchable descriptions, not global exhaustion. No complete shelf-by-shelf or image-by-image census was achieved. Unindexed catalogues, poorly described working books, constituent-unit dating and early ownership records remain substantial sources of possible additions. The near-miss register includes unresolved eligibility as well as definitive exclusions and should be used for follow-up, not as proof that every listed witness can never qualify.
